blocks.en: This course is drawn from the worship curriculum of Dr. Wayne Cook, who served eleven years as Professor of Pastoral Ministries and Preaching, together with the teaching of Andi Cook, who taught alongside him at the seminary. It reflects not only academic study but decades of pastoral and seminary experience.

Refleja no solo el estudio académico sino décadas de experiencia pastoral y de seminario.

blocks.en: I. Worship Before the Bible: Pagan and Biblical
blocks.es_reference: I. La adoración antes de la Biblia: pagana y bíblica

blocks.en: Worship is older than the church, older than Israel, older than recorded history. It is part of human nature, found in every culture and every religion that has ever existed. People have always worshipped some object, and most often that object has been drawn from nature, the sun, the storm, the river, the mountain. So what makes biblical worship different from pagan worship? Franklin Segler answers in one word: revelation. The pagan gropes in the dark and invents a god out of nature and imagination. The biblical worshipper responds to a God who has stepped forward and revealed Himself. Pagan worship reaches up and guesses; biblical worship answers a God who has spoken first.
blocks.es_reference: La adoración es más antigua que la iglesia, más antigua que Israel, más antigua que la historia registrada. Es parte de la naturaleza humana, hallada en cada cultura y cada religión que jamás ha existido. Las personas siempre han adorado algún objeto, y muy a menudo ese objeto ha sido tomado de la naturaleza, el sol, la tormenta, el río, la montaña. Entonces, ¿qué hace diferente la adoración bíblica de la pagana? Franklin Segler responde en una palabra: la revelación. El pagano tantea en la oscuridad e inventa un dios de la naturaleza y la imaginación. El adorador bíblico responde a un Dios que se ha adelantado y se ha revelado. La adoración pagana se extiende hacia arriba y adivina; la adoración bíblica responde a un Dios que ha hablado primero.

blocks.en: II. Old Testament Worship: Tabernacle and Temple
blocks.es_reference: II. La adoración del Antiguo Testamento: tabernáculo y templo

blocks.en: Old Testament worship centered first on the tabernacle and later on the temple. Even in the time of Moses, God made detailed provision for worship, and much of the Pentateuch concerns the tabernacle and the priesthood. When Solomon built the temple, the offering of sacrifices became its most important feature. The blood of bulls and goats could never take away sin, but it pointed forward to the Lamb who would. The Psalms were sung, chanted, and recited in the temple, and we still sing the Psalms in our praise today, a direct line from Solomon's temple to your congregation on Sunday morning.
blocks.es_reference: La adoración del Antiguo Testamento se centró primero en el tabernáculo y después en el templo. Aun en tiempos de Moisés, Dios hizo provisión detallada para la adoración, y gran parte del Pentateuco trata del tabernáculo y el sacerdocio. Cuando Salomón edificó el templo, la ofrenda de sacrificios se volvió su característica más importante. La sangre de toros y machos cabríos nunca pudo quitar el pecado, pero señalaba hacia adelante al Cordero que lo haría. Los Salmos se cantaban, entonaban, y recitaban en el templo, y todavía cantamos los Salmos en nuestra alabanza hoy, una línea directa desde el templo de Salomón hasta su congregación el domingo por la mañana.

blocks.en: During the Babylonian captivity, when the temple lay in ruins and the people were far from Jerusalem, a new institution arose: the synagogue. It served two purposes at once, teaching and worship. The synagogue service was informal, led by the ruler of the synagogue. They read the Scriptures, prayed, gave exhortation, recited the Shema, and answered with Amens. This is the worship Jesus knew. Luke 4:16 tells us He went into the synagogue "as His custom was." The reading of Scripture and the exposition that mark our services today come straight from the synagogue.
blocks.es_reference: Durante el cautiverio babilónico, cuando el templo yacía en ruinas y el pueblo estaba lejos de Jerusalén, surgió una nueva institución: la sinagoga. Servía dos propósitos a la vez, la enseñanza y la adoración. El servicio de la sinagoga era informal, dirigido por el principal de la sinagoga. Leían las Escrituras, oraban, daban exhortación, recitaban el Shema, y respondían con Amenes. Esta es la adoración que Jesús conoció. Lucas 4:16 nos dice que entró en la sinagoga "conforme a su costumbre." La lectura de la Escritura y la exposición que marcan nuestros servicios hoy vienen directamente de la sinagoga.

blocks.en: III. New Testament Worship and the First Day
blocks.es_reference: III. La adoración del Nuevo Testamento y el primer día

blocks.en: The first Christians were Jews who still worshipped on the Sabbath, but very quickly they began to gather on Sunday, the first day of the week, to remember the resurrection. This became the Lord's Day. Already in Colossians 2 Paul has to tell the believers to let no one judge them regarding a Sabbath day, which means the change to Sunday worship was being questioned even then. The resurrection is the reason the church gathers on the first day of the week.
blocks.es_reference: Los primeros cristianos eran judíos que todavía adoraban en el sábado, pero muy rápidamente comenzaron a reunirse el domingo, el primer día de la semana, para recordar la resurrección. Este se volvió el Día del Señor. Ya en Colosenses 2 Pablo tiene que decir a los creyentes que nadie los juzgue respecto a un día de sábado, lo que significa que el cambio a la adoración dominical estaba siendo cuestionado aun entonces. La resurrección es la razón por la que la iglesia se reúne el primer día de la semana.

blocks.en: New Testament worship had several recognizable elements: hymns, both the Psalms and new compositions like the hymn in Philippians 2; the two ordinances of baptism and the Lord's Supper; congregational Amens; the preaching of the word; and the offering for the needy. The believers sang, broke bread often, baptized new converts promptly, and gave generously. The shape of our worship today is already visible in the book of Acts.
blocks.es_reference: La adoración del Nuevo Testamento tenía varios elementos reconocibles: himnos, tanto los Salmos como nuevas composiciones como el himno en Filipenses 2; las dos ordenanzas del bautismo y la Cena del Señor; Amenes congregacionales; la predicación de la palabra; y la ofrenda para los necesitados. Los creyentes cantaban, partían el pan a menudo, bautizaban a los nuevos convertidos prontamente, y daban generosamente. La forma de nuestra adoración hoy ya es visible en el libro de Hechos.

blocks.en: IV. The Early Church and Its Corruption
blocks.es_reference: IV. La iglesia primitiva y su corrupción

blocks.en: The first broad outline of a Christian worship service comes to us from Justin Martyr, writing around AD 140. He describes the Sunday assembly: the memoirs of the apostles and the writings of the prophets are read, the president gives a discourse, all rise and pray, bread and wine are brought, the people say Amen, and the deacons carry a portion to the absent. It is a simple, beautiful, recognizable service.
blocks.es_reference: El primer bosquejo amplio de un servicio de adoración cristiana nos llega de Justino Mártir, escribiendo alrededor del año 140. Describe la asamblea dominical: se leen las memorias de los apóstoles y los escritos de los profetas, el presidente da un discurso, todos se levantan y oran, se traen pan y vino, el pueblo dice Amén, y los diáconos llevan una porción a los ausentes. Es un servicio sencillo, hermoso, reconocible.

blocks.en: Then came Constantine. In the fourth century Christianity became the legal religion of the empire, and the effect on worship was mixed at best. Crowds entered the church automatically, including unregenerate pagans baptized without conversion. Elaborate basilicas replaced humble homes, the clergy began to wear distinctive dress, and the culture began to mold the church instead of the church molding the culture. The Eucharist shifted from joy to fear and awe, ornamentation increased, and by the fifth century preaching had collapsed while tradition was elevated above Scripture. Three corruptions followed: the church was sacramentalized (salvation through seven sacraments and a bank of merit), clericalized (the priesthood of believers lost to a priestly class), and institutionalized (a living body hardened into an organization). Against all of this, Baptists hold a free church tradition, no fixed liturgy like the Book of Common Prayer, but the latitude of the apostolic church, where no fixed order even appeared until around AD 215.
blocks.es_reference: Luego vino Constantino. En el siglo cuarto el cristianismo se volvió la religión legal del imperio, y el efecto sobre la adoración fue mixto en el mejor de los casos. Las multitudes entraron a la iglesia automáticamente, incluyendo paganos inconversos bautizados sin conversión. Basílicas elaboradas reemplazaron los humildes hogares, el clero comenzó a vestir ropa distintiva, y la cultura comenzó a moldear a la iglesia en lugar de que la iglesia moldeara la cultura. La Eucaristía cambió de gozo a temor y asombro, la ornamentación aumentó, y para el siglo quinto la predicación había colapsado mientras la tradición era elevada sobre la Escritura. Siguieron tres corrupciones: la iglesia fue sacramentalizada (salvación por siete sacramentos y un banco de mérito), clericalizada (el sacerdocio de los creyentes perdido ante una clase sacerdotal), e institucionalizada (un cuerpo vivo endurecido en una organización). Contra todo esto, los bautistas sostienen una tradición de iglesia libre, sin liturgia fija como el Libro de Oración Común, sino la latitud de la iglesia apostólica, donde ni siquiera apareció un orden fijo hasta alrededor del año 215.

sa.prompt: Worship is found in every culture. Explain the difference between pagan worship and biblical worship, using Segler.
sa.model: Segler answers the difference between pagan and biblical worship in one word: revelation. Pagan worship reaches up and guesses, inventing a god out of nature and imagination, drawing its object from things like the sun, storm, river, or mountain. Biblical worship instead responds to a God who has stepped forward and revealed Himself, answering a God who has spoken first rather than a god humanity invented.

sa.prompt: Describe Old Testament worship centered on the tabernacle and temple. What was its most important feature, and what carries over into Christian worship?
sa.model: Old Testament worship centered first on the tabernacle under Moses, and later on Solomon's temple, where the offering of sacrifices became its most important feature — the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sin but pointed forward to the Lamb who would. The Psalms, sung and recited in the temple, carry directly over into Christian worship, since we still sing the Psalms today.

sa.prompt: Explain the origin and character of synagogue worship, and how Jesus related to it.
sa.model: The synagogue arose during the Babylonian captivity, when the temple lay in ruins and the people were far from Jerusalem, serving two purposes at once: teaching and worship. Its informal service included reading Scripture, prayer, exhortation, and the Shema, led by the ruler of the synagogue. Jesus knew this worship well; Luke 4:16 tells us He went into the synagogue 'as His custom was,' and much of our modern Scripture-reading and exposition traces back to it.

sa.prompt: Why did Christians move their worship from the Sabbath to Sunday, the first day of the week?
sa.model: Christians moved their worship from the Sabbath to Sunday, the first day of the week, to remember the resurrection of Christ, which had occurred on that day. This became known as the Lord's Day. The change was already being questioned even in the apostolic period, since Paul in Colossians 2 had to tell believers to let no one judge them regarding a Sabbath day.

sa.prompt: List and explain the elements of New Testament worship.
sa.model: New Testament worship included several recognizable elements: hymns, both the Psalms and new compositions like the hymn in Philippians 2; the two ordinances of baptism and the Lord's Supper; congregational Amens; the preaching of the word; and the offering for the needy. The believers sang, broke bread often, baptized new converts promptly, and gave generously — the same basic shape visible in worship today.

sa.prompt: Describe the worship service Justin Martyr outlines in his Apology around AD 140.
sa.model: Justin Martyr, writing around AD 140, describes the Sunday assembly: the memoirs of the apostles and the writings of the prophets are read, the president gives a discourse, all rise and pray, bread and wine are brought, the people say Amen, and the deacons carry a portion to the absent. It is one of the earliest broad outlines of a Christian worship service, simple and recognizable.

sa.prompt: Explain how Constantine's legalization of Christianity in the fourth century affected worship.
sa.model: Constantine's legalization of Christianity in the fourth century had a mixed effect on worship. Crowds entered the church automatically, including unregenerate pagans baptized without conversion, elaborate basilicas replaced humble homes, the clergy began to wear distinctive dress, and the surrounding culture began to shape the church instead of the church shaping the culture.

sa.prompt: How did the Eucharist and preaching change in the fourth and fifth centuries?
sa.model: In the fourth and fifth centuries, the Eucharist shifted from joy to fear and awe, and ornamentation increased around it. Preaching, meanwhile, collapsed by the fifth century while tradition was elevated above Scripture, marking a significant departure from the simple, word-centered worship of the earlier church.

sa.prompt: Explain the three key developments that corrupted the church: sacramentalized, clericalized, and institutionalized.
sa.model: Three corruptions followed the church's rise to imperial favor: it was sacramentalized, teaching salvation through seven sacraments and a bank of merit rather than grace through faith alone; clericalized, losing the priesthood of all believers to a separate priestly class; and institutionalized, hardening a living body into a rigid organization rather than a living, Spirit-led community.

sa.prompt: Explain the free church tradition and how it differs from a fixed liturgy.
sa.model: The free church tradition holds no fixed liturgy like the Book of Common Prayer, but instead the latitude of the apostolic church, where no fixed order even appeared until around AD 215. This differs from a fixed liturgy, which prescribes set words and forms for every service; a free church tradition allows the local congregation and the Spirit's leading more room to shape the shape of worship.
